source.title: Double Descent and Overparameterization in Particle Physics Data

record.file_problem: None; the full paper text is present and readable.
record.tranche_reason: The paper directly sweeps model size and training time and measures test loss/error, reproducing the double-descent tests in new particle-physics tasks and datasets.
record.gate_note: The paper reports its own model-size and epoch sweeps, so these findings are included. It cites double-descent findings from other work, which are not recorded as results here. Dataset size is varied as a condition in model-size experiments, but the paper does not report a direct test-error sweep over sample size at fixed capacity near the interpolation threshold.
record.test_reason: The study runs its own model-width and epoch sweeps on particle-physics data (jet pT regression with a transformer, event classification with MLPs) and reports test loss/error curves. This is the original recipe (width and epoch sweeps, Adam, no regularization) applied in a new domain, so T3 fits better than T1.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right but needs one correction. The authors conclude that model-wise and epoch-wise double descent occur in particle-physics data, and that this depends on task, dataset, class prior and early stopping. Overparameterized models outperform the classical regime only in the early-stopped 150k-event, 15-way case. At the final checkpoint in all cases, the second descent does not beat the classical regime.
record.recipe_differences: The study uses model-width and epoch sweeps with test-loss/error measurements, but applies them to particle-physics datasets and tasks using transformers and MLPs.
record.method_sensitivity: Task and dataset conditions affect the observed curves: epoch-wise double descent appears for the 7M unbalanced classification dataset but not the 800k balanced one; under early stopping, the model-wise peak is absent for 3k events and appears for 150k events.
record.problems: The paper provides no uncertainty estimates in the supplied text. Several outcomes are described qualitatively and their plotted values are not tabulated. The reported behavior is task- and dataset-dependent.

untested.parts: No label-noise variation, and no domains beyond the two particle-physics datasets. Only three architectures/tasks are tested.
No label-noise manipulation. The balance-vs-size confound is not disentangled.
Dataset size differs across experiments, but always together with changes in architecture and task. There is no sample-size sweep at fixed capacity.
No label-noise or regularization sweeps (weight decay is zero throughout). No multiple peaks are studied.
No effective-parameter re-expression of the curves.

record.verdict_notes: Short workshop-style preprint. Results are qualitative and figure-only, with no uncertainty estimates or seeds reported. Early stopping selects the best test-set checkpoint, which is optimistic. Double descent appears without injected label noise and without regularization; this is not a direct test of V6. The relation is reclassified from T1 to T3 because it is a new-domain replication.

versions.untested_parts: The paper tests model-wise double descent in particle-physics tasks, not across all deep-network settings.
The paper tests epoch-wise behavior in the reported regression and classification tasks, not across other tasks or training setups.
No direct test-error comparison varying sample count at fixed model capacity near the interpolation threshold is reported.
The study tests neural networks only; it does not test whether the curve generalizes across model classes.
No single effective-complexity measure predicting peak locations across size, epochs, and sample count is tested.
The study does not test label-noise or regularization dependence, multiple peaks, or disappearance under optimally tuned regularization.
The study does not re-express the curves using an effective parameter count or test whether this makes the second descent an ordinary U-shaped curve.

rows.subject: permutation equivariant two-layer transformer
rows.operation_detail: Sweep model width and compare test MSE.
rows.value: The paper reports model-wise double descent, with the test loss worst at the interpolation threshold and decreasing again for large models; the second descent does not outperform the classical regime.
rows.note: The text describes the curve and its relation to the interpolation threshold; plotted numerical values are not reported in the text.
rows.check: Correct. The text says test loss is worst at the interpolation threshold and decreases again for large models; the second descent does not beat the classical regime. Values are plotted only.

rows.operation_detail: Track test loss over training epochs.
rows.value: Test performance first improves, then worsens, and improves again after the training data is memorized.
rows.note: The paper explicitly describes epoch-wise double descent.
rows.check: Correct. Fig. 1c slices at dmodel 8/128/1024; the text describes improve, overfit, improve again after memorization.

rows.subject: 3-layer MLP
rows.operation_detail: Track test error over training epochs.
rows.value: The large models on the balanced dataset do not exhibit epoch-wise double descent.
rows.note: The paper states this outcome for the large models shown; it does not give numeric trajectory values in the text.
rows.check: State is right, but the condition is confounded. The balanced (800k) and unbalanced (7M) datasets differ in both class prior and sample size. The authors attribute the difference to imbalance only as a hypothesis.

rows.note: The paper reports the balanced and unbalanced training conditions as differing in whether epoch-wise double descent appears.
rows.check: Correct. Same confound with R3: the 7M unbalanced set differs in size as well as class prior.

rows.value: The generalization penalty at the interpolation peak disappears; test performance improves monotonically for heavily overparameterized models.

rows.value: A temporary increase in generalization error appears around the interpolation threshold, followed by a second descent; high-capacity models outperform the classical regime.
rows.note: The paper reports the double-descent pattern and an overparameterization benefit under this early-stopping condition.
rows.check: The early-stopping checkpoint is selected on the test set. High-capacity models (up to ~1.1B parameters) outperform the classical regime.
